signal.title: Show HN: MCPJam - the first testing & evaluations platform for MCP servers
signal.text: Prathmesh, CEO of MCPJam here. Users now start in ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor, and other AI clients. They reach your product through your MCP server. That means your users often aren’t in your product anymore. You can’t see what they prompted for, how the agent interpreted it, or whether your server helped them get the result they wanted. I saw this firsthand leading MCP technical strategy at Asana, including our ChatGPT and Claude launches. We were building high-stakes enterprise integrations, but we had no reliable way to test them the way we test normal software- or to know whether they worked once they reached real users. I started using MCPJam for those problems after re-connecting with my former coworker who created the project. brought it to more of our developers, and worked it into our CI/CD pipeline. I joined the team because I kept hearing the same issue from other companies building for agents. So, what does “good” look like for MCP? For us, it means users reliably get the outcome they came for, across the AI clients they use. That’s what we’ve been building toward. MCPJam now helps you test the full workflow, from the first prompt to the expected result: * Swarms: Simulate users with different goals and prompts to find where workflows break across AI clients. * User Testing: Watch how real users interact with your MCP product, where they get stuck, and how they feel about the results. * Evals: Turn those workflows into repeatable tests that check whether users get the expected outcome. * CI/CD: Run those evals across AI clients before each release to catch regressions. Over 106,000 developers and +300 enterprises use our open-source solution to see how their servers behave locally across major AI clients. MCPJam has grown from a debugging tool into a continuous testing and evaluation workflow for MCP servers. If you’re building an MCP server or agent-facing product, give MCPJam a try. What is the hardest thing for you to test? We love hearing about your MCP server builds!

signal.title: Show HN: Formstep, Request information from customers without the back-and-forth
signal.text: I built Formstep: https://formstep.io The idea came from a problem I kept running into while working on loan applications. A workflow could automate a large part of the process, but eventually it would need something only the customer could provide: a document, a correction, a signature, an explanation, or confirmation of some information. At that point, workflow automation basically did not work. The forms themselves were also often the source of the problem. Applications came in with wrong documents, misunderstood questions, incomplete answers, or people simply forgetting to finish. Someone had to email the customer, explain what was missing, wait for a reply then follow up again. It was always back-and-forth. So I built Formstep to make requesting information from customers easier, not only for humans, but also for workflows and AI agents. The idea is: A person, workflow, or AI agent sends a customer a request through email or a link. Either re-use existing form or create unique for each customer. You can prefill what you already know, lock fields, pass context, and only ask the customer what you need. For example, we might already know: * Address that you already have in the CRM * Company description from the internet * What a agreement document must contain * How a good answer should be Formstep can check inputs and uploaded files while the customer is filling out the form and tell them if something is missing or inconsistent before they submit. For example “The PDF does not contain your signature” or “Invoice total does not match the order amount”. The goal is to catch problems while the customer is still there, rather than letting bad data continue through the workflow and discovering it later. On the automation side, requests can currently be created through n8n, Zapier, the REST API, or by an AI agent over MCP. When the customer finishes, the structured answers can go back into the workflow so it can continue. Forms and invitation/reminder are multilingual, and submitted answers can be translated inside the dashboard with one click. If you want, Formstep can be used as normal form builder and shared through public links, QR, embeds etc. It support custom themes for dark/light mode, with cover image, has Notion-style editor and much more. The list is too long to fit here. I want to make Formstep a plattform where it becomes more intelligent over time and ensures that we can get better answers from customers for any use case. My question to you: Where do your automations currently stop because they need input from a customer or user, and how are you handling that today? If you are interested in trying out the n8n node: https://www.npmjs.com/package/n8n-nodes-formstep Zapier integration: https://zapier.com/apps/formstep/integrations Connecting your AI agent: https://docs.formstep.io/developers/mcp-server/ Docs: https://docs.formstep.io I would love your feedback and please try a quick demo at https://app.formstep.io/try

signal.title: Show HN: Frink – Desktop-first app for multi-step workflows and parallel agents
signal.text: What’s up HN?! I'm Benji, and I’ve been building Frink since ~April this year. Frink is a desktop-first, open-source (MIT) app for running coding agents in parallel and multi-step workflows that start on their own. It runs on your machine (macOS and Linux) with your own provider login. It currently supports Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot, and OpenCode, but the latter 3 are in preview. No Frink account to use the app. The biggest USP of Frink is workflows: think n8n for agents. You describe a routine in a sentence, for example: "every weekday at 9am, run the tests; if any fail, have an agent fix them, then wait for my approval before it opens a PR." Then, Frink builds it as a workflow (or simply, Flow): a list of steps you can read and change before it runs. A Flow can start on a schedule, from any webhook, or from an event from a third-party such as Linear, Shortcut, ClickUp, Sentry, PostHog, etc. Steps can be agent turns, shell commands, conditions, approval steps that stop and wait for you, or steps you write yourself in code (or ask the agent to write one). Everything that needs you (an approval, an agent's question, a finished task to review) lands in one Work Queue. Other stuff: * Up to four agents side by side, each on its own git worktree if you want. Or, many agents out of direct view. * Every change shows as a diff; there's a code editor, a terminal, etc. * Local-first: chats, Flows and tasks live in SQLite on your machine. * Easier provider parity: currently working on and improving the tooling setup between providers. Once inside Frink, irrespective of what provider you use, the hooks, MCPs, and other tooling work out of the box between providers. Why I built it: I started building it when there weren’t many other competitors; now the industry is swamped with ADEs and harnesses. However, in my opinion, each still lacks good automation for more fine-tuned scenarios. I doubled down on the flows to help me with my actual day-to-day job as a SWE, and over time it’s helped me automate most of the PRs being shipped across my personal projects, team, etc., to the point that it’s a continuous loop and helps a whole ton. Notes: Windows isn't supported yet. Flows only run on Claude Code and Codex for now. It's a solo project, so expect sharp edges.

signal.title: Wiki-driven development: coding agents update a wiki for you, you set direction
signal.text: My team has been working in a way we are calling calling wiki-driven development, where the wiki is written for the human, not the agent and the human uses primarily the wiki to set direction for the agent. This is different from Karparthy's LLm I'm curious whether others do something like it. Once I run several coding agents at a time, I get overwhelmed and disorganized. Every session makes decisions and raises questions, and I can't reread the transcripts. CLAUDE.md and agent memory help the agent, but they don't give me a place to see what is going on and decide. The problem gets worse with a team. So, I have the agents write a wiki, and they write it for me. As they work, they record only what is significant: decisions with who made them, when, and the option we passed over; open questions with an owner; and a short summary of where each area stands. I ask it to focus on the big picture, strategy, key architectural or business decisions. In more detail: 1. Agents do the work and update the pages it affects with what is significant: key decisions, key strategic points, open questions, and a summary of where things stand. 2. I read the wiki to understand the big picture: the key points, where we are, and what still needs to be decided. It is short enough to read. 3. I think and decide there: I settle a question, change a decision, lay out some more strategy points, or rewrite a page to say where I want to go. 4. The next session builds from the page I changed. Karpathy's LLM Wiki idea is related, but it compiles sources you collect into a knowledge base that keeps getting richer. His goal is completeness for research. Our approach is minimalistic: the pages distill way down from the agents' sessions, hold only what is significant, and exist only so I can think and decide. Spec-driven development has you write the spec up front for the agent to implement. Here the agent writes the wiki based on all the valuable detail that are in my session prompts and its response and I edit the wiki, so the document keeps up with the agents work and my job is thinking, organizing, deciding, direction. Here are some things I have learned doing this: - Organization is key for me as the human. I make the agent make a nice visual html with clickable links marketecture or architecture or business model canvas as the top page and navigate from there. I have it keep each page a page long so I actually am motivated to read stuff. - Have the decisions record the rejected options, so when someone brings a question back, the reasoning is available. We are constantly revisiting decisions as we work and learn and so this is very helpful. - The agent wants to write everything down. The criteria I give it is to only record what it would need to get back to where we are right now in terms of strategy, decisions, implementation. Its not that much. You can do the same with a CLAUDE.md that tells the agent what to record, and work in markdown files or Obsidian or Notion. We got so into this that we turned it into a free, MIT-licensed plugin for Claude Code and Codex that keeps the wiki as markdown files in your repo and lets you see the wiki in your browser locally: https://github.com/nimbalyst/nimbalyst-wiki. Do you work in this way? If so, what other things should we be doing and how have you made it work well?

signal.title: Show HN: SchemaWright, learning database design in a gamified way
signal.text: Let me begin by explaining what it is: SchemaWright is a platform for learning database table design in a gamified way, with a real Postgres database running on your browser via WASM. It was heavily inspired by Duolingo and LeetCode, because I love the way how those platforms teach their users. I built and launched this a couple months ago, weeks after my first SaaS failed (that one was called NoteRaven, and the idea was for it to be a Notion + Medium + Udemy all in one platform; but after looking at how saturated that market was, I decided to move on). The story on how I came up with it is basically that I was working normally on my day job, and noticed how many times we had changed some core tables, and usually discussed renaming them, changing columns, relationships etc. After that, I realized that I wanted to learn how to "get the schema right" from the beginning, so I began looking for websites that could teach that. It didnt take long to realize I couldn't find one that fitted my needs: it had to feel gamified and rigorous at the same time. When I say "rigorous" I mean that the content shouldnt be standard exercises we see in university (that we never really use at work) or loose definitions we feel like is too shallow. Therefore, I decided that I would be the one to build such platform. The way I structured the app is by separating it in 3 main pages: Learn, Exercises and Lectures. The first one is where you'll find Duolingo like lessons for database schema, it goes from the foundations (what is a table, what are rows and columns), to intermediate/advanced contents, such as concurrency and queues, scaling and architecture etc. It has 8 levels, but I currently only wrote up to level 3 (normalisation). Which is funny because my boss once tested me on this lol. The Exercises page is where I took inspiratoin from LeetCode, especially the page for an exercise structure: on the left side you have the problem description, your submissions and an editorial, and on the right side the code editor and the tests that will run on your code. Finally the last page is for people who are keen on reading papers and are more drawn to academic research. The lectures reference famous and important research papers that led us to our current understanding of databases, sql and concepts we learn today on this subject. It summarizes them and teaches you the concepts, while containing some interactive exercises too! Ok, so why do I think this may work as opposed to NoteRaven? One of the reasons is that I shared this with my co-workers (60+ people, most are devs too) and boss (who is CEO and CTO), and they really enjoyed using it. That same boss gave me positive feedback and suggestions, that I actually ended up implementing on the platform (yeah your suggestion could end up there too!). Another would be that I feel like platforms that train you on database design are scarce compared to ones that teach you queries, so the market wouldn't be so saturated. Let me know what you guys think! Please share if you think some exercises are unfair, meaning that they need better context for people to answer them, and also what you think of the lesson's pace, content and interactive exercises; the same goes for the lectures.

signal.title: Show HN: Mnemify – 3D terrain map merging Confluence, Notion, Obsidian
signal.text: I have been working on documents for last 5 years. Recently I realized I was using Confluence to structure execution notes, Notion for thoughts during meetings, Obsidian for quick local notes, and then reading back notes from Googles note taking apps. My colleague had the exact same problem. We had MCP connected to Claude, but there was no way to bring all of that into one place that was intuitive. So we built Mnemify. Which converted all our notes from every app to a 3D traversable terrain instead. We’ve been using it daily for last two months and found it useful so decided to share it. What it does: it harvests your sources into a local folder, then using your AI subscriptions compiles them into a 3D terrain you can traverse. Regions and peaks come from context, so related things end up adjacent from all your connected apps. We also have chat over the compiled graph that cites the exact source passages. You can also view time wise how the terrain was modified over time and see all your note higlights and action items in workspaces. Everything stays on your machine. It never writes back to any source. Models are bring your own: OpenAI, Claude (your claude CLI or a subscription), or a fully offline mode with an on-device embedding model. Currently supported sources: Confluence, Notion, Obsidian and local files. Jira, Linear, Slack, Gmail and Google Meet notes are built and coming... Please try it out, would appreciate your feedback. Repo: https://github.com/mnemify-ai/mnemify Our Landing: https://mnemify.ai
